lines: Ten demos, made with a computer mouse. Sloppy ones.
Copy them directly, and the robot fails all forty test scenes.
Run them through SANT, and it succeeds thirty out of forty, on scenes it had never seen.
Robots learn new skills by copying people, and good demonstrations are expensive: a teleoperation rig, a trained operator, take after take.
Cheap demos, from a mouse or a webcam, are easy to get, but sloppy. They pause, they wobble, they grab off centre.
Our ten webcam demos all put the cube in the bin, and physics rejected every one. This one pressed into the bin with nine hundred and twenty-seven newtons. The limit is five.
NVIDIA's tools, like Isaac Lab Mimic, multiply demos that already work. SANT is the step before: it turns cheap, sloppy demos into ones worth multiplying.
Simulate, Augment, Neaten, Train. It runs on NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, with Nemotron on Nebius Token Factory.
You record a demo in the browser. Your mouse, keyboard or webcam drives a Franka arm inside Isaac Lab, live.
Then SANT takes over. It replays every demo with real contact forces, and code decides whether it actually worked.
Demos that fail get repaired, by tested rules or with fixes Nemotron proposes, and every fix is checked in physics again.
Then it multiplies. The cube and the bin move, every copy is replayed, and only the copies that pass are kept.
Nemotron labels demos, turns a sentence into a scene, and proposes repairs. It never moves the robot. Code checks every answer, and physics has the final word.
Because Token Factory hosts the models, our one GPU stayed free for Isaac Lab. Four hundred and eighty-three calls cost about a dollar fourteen.
But copying even clean, verified demos stalled at three out of forty.
So a reinforcement-learning teacher practises in Isaac Lab, four thousand arms at once, starting from the human demos.
Without the demos, the same teacher never lifted the cube. Zero out of a hundred and twenty-eight, against a hundred and thirteen with them.
SANT checked the teacher too. Its first good version moved at one point seven metres a second, and only three of fifty runs held up. Capped, all fifty passed.
The teacher's skill is distilled into a robot that sees only through cameras. These are its real test runs, replayed from Isaac.
Forty fresh scenes, one try, and a goal of twenty-four, written down before the run. It got thirty.
All ten failures were drops. That's what we fix next.
Everything here is simulation: one task, one arm. A real robot is next.
Ten sloppy demos in. A robot that works out. This is SANT.
